findings.issue_text: pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:45 — [P2, confidence 100] `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil { return ret, nil }` followed by unconditional `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` omits a cache recheck under the write lock, so a concurrent production cold-start burst serially rereads the same manifest once per waiting request and startup latency grows with request count.

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — [P2 advisory, confidence 100] `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` is taken for every development request and held across manifest I/O, so concurrent development requests are forced through a process-wide serialization point even though that environment deliberately bypasses the cache; the counterargument that manifest reads are cheap does not survive slow or remote filesystems, and moving the development path outside the cache lock deletes this contention branch.

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:36 — [P2 advisory, confidence 50] `entryPointAssetsCacheMu sync.RWMutex` guards a process-global cache that is not keyed by `cfg.StaticRootPath` or the license-derived CDN prefix, so the first non-development caller's asset paths are returned to every later caller using a different configuration; the counterargument that production normally has one configuration does not survive tests, embedded servers, or multi-instance process use allowed by the function's explicit per-call configuration argument, and owning the cache per configured service instance makes the global mutex and cache unnecessary.

docs/tasks/task-001.md:2 — [P1, confidence 100] `Review the change.` defines no acceptance criteria for the new cache synchronization, so completion cannot establish whether concurrent cold-cache calls must perform one manifest load, preserve development-mode reload behavior, or retry after load errors.

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:41 — [P2, confidence 100] `ret := entryPointAssetsCache` is captured before acquiring the write lock and never rechecked, so every request in a concurrent cold-start burst that observed nil serially rereads the manifest under the exclusive lock after the first request has populated the cache, amplifying startup I/O and request latency instead of coalescing the work.

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — [P2 advisory, confidence 100] `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` wraps the entire manifest read even when `cfg.Env == setting.Dev`, so concurrent development requests are forced through one-at-a-time filesystem I/O and a slow or stalled read blocks every other caller despite caching being disabled.

goldens.comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in development mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), the code will acquire the write lock (entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()) on every request since the cache is bypassed. The diff shows that after the RLock/RUnlock check, if we're in dev mode OR cache is nil, we proceed to take the full Lock and hold it through the manifest I/O operations. This is a valid performance/architecture concern - dev requests serialize unnecessarily. However, this is not a bug (dev mode still works correctly), but rather a design issue that could cause contention. The finding is specific and grounded in the actual diff code.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real architectural concern: the global cache is not keyed by configuration parameters (cfg.StaticRootPath or license-derived CDN prefix), yet the function accepts per-call configuration. The diff shows GetWebAssets takes cfg and license as parameters, but the cache is a single global variable. This means if the function is called with different configurations (e.g., in tests or multi-instance scenarios), the first caller's cached result would be returned to subsequent callers with different configs. This is a legitimate design/architecture concern introduced by adding thread-safety to an already-problematic global cache pattern, though it's not strictly a bug introduced by this diff (the caching issue existed before, this diff just adds mutex protection). The TODO comment in the diff acknowledges 'get rid of global state' suggesting awareness of this issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:41 — [P2, confidence 100] `ret := entryPointAssetsCache` is captured before acquiring the write lock and never rechecked, so every request in a concurrent cold-start burst that observed nil serially rereads the manifest under the exclusive lock after the first request has populated the cache, amplifying startup I/O and request latency instead of coalescing the work.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the diff: after releasing the RLock and before acquiring the Lock, the code doesn't recheck if the cache was populated by another goroutine. This means multiple concurrent requests during cold-start will all proceed to read the manifest file even though only the first one needs to. This is a valid double-checked locking pattern issue - the code should recheck `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write lock. However, this is a performance/efficiency concern rather than a correctness bug - the code will still work correctly, just with redundant I/O during startup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — [P2 advisory, confidence 100] `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` wraps the entire manifest read even when `cfg.Env == setting.Dev`, so concurrent development requests are forced through one-at-a-time filesystem I/O and a slow or stalled read blocks every other caller despite caching being disabled.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in Dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), the code still acquires the write lock (entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()) before reading the manifest, even though caching is disabled. This means concurrent requests in development will serialize on filesystem I/O. This is a valid architectural/performance concern grounded in the diff - the lock is acquired unconditionally after the early return check fails. However, this is not a bug per se - it's a design tradeoff that affects development performance but doesn't cause incorrect behavior.
